title: Getting to know someone
grammar: Questions: yes/no questions and question words
summary: Yes/no question: verb first, then the subject (Woon je hier?). With a question word: question word, verb, subject (Waar woon je?). Welke with de-words and plurals, welk with het-words. Jij after the verb loses its t.
explain:
Dutch makes a question by changing the word order: the verb moves in front of the subject. There is no helper verb like English *do*. There are two kinds of question, and in both the subject comes **directly after the verb**.

### Yes/no questions: the verb first

A question that you answer with ja or nee starts with the conjugated verb. Then comes the subject, then the rest.

> Woon je hier al lang? — Have you lived here long?
> Spreekt u Engels? — Do you (formal) speak English?
> Zijn jullie hier ook nieuw? — Are you (plural) new here too?

Jij and je after the verb make it lose its t, as in unit A2 · 1: `jij woont`, but `Woon jij hier?` `Hij` and `u` keep the t: `Woont hij hier?`, `Woont u hier?`

### Questions with a question word

The question word goes first, then the verb, then the subject. It is the rule of unit A2 · 3: the question word is element number one, the verb number two.

| question word | meaning | example |
| wie | who | Wie is dat? |
| wat | what | Wat doe je? |
| waar | where | Waar woon je? |
| wanneer | when | Wanneer begin je? |
| waarom | why | Waarom lach je? |
| hoe | how | Hoe gaat het? |
| hoeveel | how much, how many | Hoeveel kinderen heeft u? |
| hoe laat | what time | Hoe laat is het? |
| hoe lang | how long | Hoe lang blijf je? |
| hoe vaak | how often | Hoe vaak sport je? |
| hoe oud | how old | Hoe oud is hij? |

> Hoe lang woont u al in Nederland? — How long have you (formal) lived in the Netherlands?

### Welk or welke, and wat voor

`Welke` (which) goes with de-words and with every plural. `Welk` goes only with a het-word in the singular.

> Welke taal spreek je thuis? — Which language do you speak at home? (de taal)
> Uit welk land kom je? — Which country are you from? (het land)

`Wat voor` asks what kind: `Wat voor werk doe je?` With a singular noun you can count, `een` is often added: `Wat voor (een) auto heb je?` With plurals and with nouns you cannot count there is no een: `Wat voor boeken lees je?`

### Waar … vandaan and waar … naartoe

These question words are split: `waar` goes first, and `vandaan` (from) or `naartoe` (to) goes to the **end**. Instead of naartoe you can also say `heen`.

> Waar kom je vandaan? — Where are you from?
> Waar gaan jullie in de zomer naartoe? — Where are you (plural) going in the summer?

### Wie or wat as the subject

When `wie` or `wat` is itself the subject, the verb follows it directly, and it is normally singular, even if the answer could be several people.

> Wie woont hier? — Who lives here?

But in `Wie zijn die mensen?` the subject is `die mensen`, so the verb is plural.

### A preposition goes in front

English puts the preposition at the end (*Who do you live with?*). Dutch puts it in front of `wie`: `Met wie woon je?`, `Van wie is die jas?` For things, Dutch usually says `waarmee`, `waarover` and so on (more in B1).

### Answering: ja, nee and jawel

To say yes to a negative question, and so contradict it, Dutch uses `jawel`. `Ja` alone sounds unclear, and `nee` agrees with the negative.

> Ben je niet moe? Jawel, heel erg. — Aren't you tired? Yes, I am, very.

### Watch out

- The verb comes before the subject: *Waar jij woont? → `Waar woon jij?`
- The t goes: *Woont jij hier? → `Woon jij hier?`
- No *do*: *Doe je spreken Engels? → `Spreek je Engels?`
- *Welk taal → `Welke taal`; *Welke land → `Welk land`.
- *Waar kom je van? → `Waar kom je vandaan?`
- *Wie woon je mee? → `Met wie woon je?`

### Compared with Ukrainian

Ukrainian can make a question just with the voice or with `чи`: `Ти тут живеш?` Dutch needs the word order: `Woon jij hier?` And where Ukrainian says just `Звідки ти?`, Dutch needs a verb: `Waar kom je vandaan?`

sentences.en: How do you spell your surname?
sentences.note: Question word, verb, subject. Je comes directly after the verb, so the t of spelt disappears: spel je.
Waar goes first and vandaan goes to the very end. Between them the normal question order: verb, subject, the rest.
A yes/no question starts with the verb: is. The subject Oekraïens follows it directly.

sentences.nl: Is zij een vriendin of een kennis?
sentences.en: Is she a friend or an acquaintance?
sentences.note: The verb comes first and the subject zij second. Of only joins the two choices and changes nothing in the order.
alt: Is ze een vriendin of een kennis?

sentences.en: Which languages do you speak at home?
sentences.note: Talen is a plural, and every plural takes welke. Je after the verb: spreek, without t.

sentences.nl: In welk land ben je geboren?
sentences.en: In which country were you born?
sentences.note: Land is a het-word in the singular, so welk without e. The preposition in goes in front of the question word.
alt: In welk land ben jij geboren?

sentences.en: What kind of work do you do?
sentences.note: Wat voor asks what kind. Werk is a noun you cannot count, so there is no een.
Wie is the subject here, so the verb follows it directly and is singular: spreekt, even if several people may answer.

sentences.nl: Aangenaam, ik ben Olena. Hoe heet jij?
sentences.en: Pleased to meet you, I am Olena. What is your name?
sentences.note: Hoe heet jij? is how Dutch asks for a name: literally 'how are you called'. Heten has a stem ending in t, so heet jij and jij heet look the same.
alt: Aangenaam, ik ben Olena. Hoe heet je?
Aangenaam, ik heet Olena. Hoe heet jij?
Aangenaam, ik heet Olena. Hoe heet je?

sentences.nl: Woon je hier niet? Jawel, al drie jaar.
sentences.en: Don't you live here? Yes, I do: for three years now.
sentences.note: The question starts with the verb: woon je, without t. To say yes to a negative question you use jawel, not ja.
alt: Woon jij hier niet? Jawel, al drie jaar.

exercises.note: After the question word comes the verb, then the subject: heten jullie. Only jij and je make the verb lose its t; jullie keeps the infinitive.

exercises.en: Which country is your (formal) husband from?
exercises.note: Land is a het-word and singular, so welk without e. Welke is for de-words and plurals; wat cannot stand before a noun like this.

exercises.en: Who knows the new neighbour already?
exercises.note: Wie is the subject, so the verb follows it directly in the singular hij-form: kent. With ken je, wie would no longer be the subject.

exercises.nl: Ben je niet moe? ___, ik ben heel moe.
exercises.en: Aren't you tired? Yes, I am very tired.
exercises.note: Jawel contradicts a negative question: yes, I am. Nee would agree with niet and mean 'no, I am not tired'.

exercises.en: What is your (formal) place of residence?
exercises.note: Wat asks for a piece of information, like a name or a place on a form. Welke only stands in front of a noun: welke stad.

exercises.en: What kind of music do you like?
exercises.note: Wat voor means 'what kind of'. Muziek cannot be counted, so there is no een after wat voor.
Je comes directly after the verb, so the t disappears: bedoel je. With hij it stays: Wat bedoelt hij?

exercises.nl: Met ___ heb je morgen een gesprek?
exercises.en: Who are you having a conversation with tomorrow?
exercises.note: For a person after a preposition Dutch uses wie, and the preposition goes in front of it: met wie. Never *wie … met at the end.

answers: Waar ga je in de zomer naartoe?
Waar ga je naartoe in de zomer?
exercises.en: Where are you going in the summer?
exercises.note: Waar first, then the verb and the subject. Naartoe normally closes the sentence; in speech the time can also follow it.
Question word, verb, subject. A short word like elkaar comes right after the subject, before meestal.

answers: Hoe lang wonen uw buren al in deze straat?
exercises.en: How long have your (formal) neighbours lived in this street?
exercises.note: Hoe lang is one question word and stands first. The verb wonen comes second and agrees with the plural subject uw buren.

exercises.task: Ask where he is from, with waar … vandaan.
exercises.note: Waar takes the first place and vandaan goes to the end. Hij keeps the t: komt hij.

exercises.task: Ask the same thing in everyday Dutch, with hoe oud.
exercises.note: Hoe oud is the question word, then the verb and the subject: bent u. Wat is uw leeftijd? is what a form says.
After the question word comes the verb, then the subject. And jij after the verb loses the t: woon jij.
Nationaliteit is a de-word, like every word in -teit, so welke. Welk is only for het-words in the singular.
In a yes/no question jij stands directly after the verb, and then the verb loses its t: woon jij.
